name: Wendy Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the overhead crew at the Kilbride depot, a little coastal town, five of us covering the town and the headland farms. Wind and salt are our whole life: salt eats the insulators, wind brings the branches down. A normal day is a pole change or a new house hook-up, and a not-normal day is a storm where we're out for thirty hours straight. My dad did this job from the same depot, and so did his dad, so I was carrying his tool belt before I could ride a bike.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people in town know us. You get a wave at the shop because their lights came back on at three in the morning. What wears me out is the new tablets they've given us, honestly, more than the storms. I've never touched one of those AI apps and I don't plan to. I live with my fiancé Rob, who's a mechanic at the garage on Quay Road, and we're getting married next autumn at St Bride's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that you can't fix a line from a computer. At the depot we'd have a laugh about all the money spent on it. I don't do online, so it'd just be the depot and maybe after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think that's about right. The job's the job. People will always need power, and somebody has to climb up and fix it when the weather has a go at the headland.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep working, keep doing my storm call-outs, and we'd keep saving for the wedding, about two hundred a month each. If they make the tablet do more of my paperwork, fine, as long as I don't have to learn anything new to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know. The only thing I'd be stressed about is the wedding seating plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet. What is it about the tablet that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wants you to tick forty boxes on a pole change. My dad wrote three lines in a notebook and the job was just as safe as a forty-box tablet. I'll do it because I have to, but I resent losing twenty minutes a day to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How settled does money feel at the moment, apart from the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. We've got about two months of bills put away, plus the wedding fund. Rob's job is steady, and the garage is the only one in town. We rent a cottage from his aunt, so the rent is fair.

say: You **can't fix a line** from a computer, so the hype was money wasted.
I'd say it at the **depot** or **after church**, never online.
think: People will **always need power**, and someone has to climb up and fix it.
The job carries on **as it is**, which feels right to me.
do: Keep working the same and take **storm call-outs** as usual.
Save **£200 a month** each with her fiancé Rob for the wedding.
Use the **tablet** only as much as she is made to.
feel: **Calm**; the only stress is the **wedding seating plan**.
S0.quote: My dad wrote three lines in a notebook and the job was just as safe as a forty-box tablet.
fieldNote: Wendy's identity is tied to **family tradition**: third generation at the same depot.
Her irritation is with **paperwork technology**, not with the work itself.
Money feels secure thanks to a **fair rent** from family and a steady partner.

steps.text: Keep taking storm call-outs on the headland as usual
Put £200 a month into the wedding fund with Rob

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people in head office should worry, not us. At the depot we'd say good, fewer clipboards. I'd be careful saying it after church, because Mrs Duffy's son does the billing for the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes how we're managed more than what we do. The planning would come from a computer, the job sheets would be checked by a computer, and nobody at head office would know the headland like we do. That bothers me more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, and I'd do the tablet training because they'd make me. I'd keep the wedding small-ish and start putting a bit more by after it. I wouldn't go chasing courses, I'm a lineworker and I want to stay one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my pay. More that the company starts being run by people who've never been up a pole in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the tablet training because they'd make you. What would you think of colleagues who took to it straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good luck to them. Young Tariq on our crew would love it, he's always on his phone. But someone has to remember how to do the job without the screen, for the day the system's down in a storm, and that'll be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible if the office jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, but that's business, they'll always go for the cheapest. I don't think the government should prop up jobs that aren't needed. I'd rather families and the parish looked after people while they found new work.

say: **Head office** should worry, not the crews out on the lines.
At the depot we'd say **fewer clipboards**, but I'd go careful near **church friends** in billing.
think: AI changes how we're **managed** more than the work itself.
Nobody at head office would **know the headland** like the crew does.
do: Do the **tablet training** only because it's required.
Keep the **wedding small-ish** and save more once it's done.
Stay a **lineworker** rather than chase courses.
feel: **Uneasy** about being run by people who have **never climbed** a pole.
S1.quote: Someone has to remember how to do the job without the screen, for the day the system's down in a storm, and that'll be me.
fieldNote: Wendy positions herself as the **keeper of old skills** when systems fail.
She accepts office job losses as **business** and prefers family and parish support over government.
Her unease is about **remote management**, not about her wage.

steps.text: Sit the required tablet training and nothing beyond it
Hold a smaller wedding and save £150 a month afterwards

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three pictures share an end point. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe a robot can do storm work on the headland. I'd say it loud at the depot. But I'd be saying it partly to calm myself down, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people by 2031 means me, and it means Rob too, because the same robots would be in the garage. A robot that can fix a power line can fix a car, so that's both our wages in one go. I'd be thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd make the wedding smaller, just the church and the hall, and put the difference in the bank. We'd stop any big spending and try to get to six months saved. I'd talk to my dad, because he knows every manager in the company, and see what he thinks we should do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Rob and I would be lying awake doing sums. I don't know what else I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your dad. What do you think he'd tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd tell me to stay put and keep my head down, because the company always needs someone in an emergency. He's never been wrong about the job before. But he's never seen anything like this, and neither has anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd look into, outside line work, in those first two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got no idea, honestly. Maybe the council, maybe the fire service, something where they need a person in the room. But I'm not someone who changes easily, and two years is nothing.

say: I'd say loudly that no robot can do **storm work** on the headland.
Part of saying it would be to **calm myself down**.
think: Robots by **2031** threaten both her job and fiancé Rob's as a mechanic.
That's **both our wages** gone in one go, when she'd be thirty.
do: Cut the wedding to **church and the hall** and bank the difference.
Stop big spending to reach **six months** of savings.
Ask her dad, who **knows every manager**, what to do.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake doing sums with Rob.
Lost about what else she's **good at**.
S2.quote: A robot that can fix a power line can fix a car, so that's both our wages in one go.
fieldNote: Wendy's **household risk** is doubled, because her fiancé's mechanic job is also hands-on.
Her loud public scepticism is partly a way to **calm herself**, which she admits.
She has **no plan B** and relies on her father's advice and family networks.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to the church and hall and bank the savings
Build savings with Rob to six months of bills
Ask her father for advice through his company contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast for a small town. At the depot I'd say we should all stick together and make sure the company keeps people on storm duty. Mostly I'd say it to Rob.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it gives me a bit of breathing room. The thinking stuff goes in 2031, but that's the office, and the robots wouldn't come until 2034. I'd be thirty-four, maybe with a baby, and I'm not sure where that leaves me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have the proper wedding, but we'd hold off buying a house until we see how it goes. I'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month, and keep my head down at work. If the company offered a course in looking after the robots, I might do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. It feels like something coming up the road that you can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe with a baby. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might push them back a year or two. My mum had me at twenty-six and always said you never feel ready anyway. But I wouldn't want a baby the same year my job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might do a course if the company offered one. Why not go looking for one yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be guessing. I don't trust any of these colleges selling courses for jobs that don't exist yet. If the company needs people for the robots, they'll train their own, and I'd rather be picked than chase it.

say: Five years is still **too fast** for a small town.
The crew should **stick together** so the company keeps people on **storm duty**.
think: There's **breathing room**, since robots wouldn't come until 2034.
At **thirty-four**, maybe with a baby, she's unsure where that leaves her.
do: Hold off **buying a house** until the picture is clearer.
Save about **£300 a month** and keep her head down at work.
Push **having a baby** back a year or two.
feel: **Worried**, like something coming up the road you **can't stop**.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want a baby the same year my job disappears.
fieldNote: Extra time lets Wendy keep the **wedding** but delay the house and children.
She distrusts **colleges selling courses** and would only retrain if the company chose her.
Her strategy is **waiting to be picked**, consistent with her resistance to change.

steps.text: Save £300 a month and hold off buying a house
Delay trying for a baby by a year or two
Wait for the company to offer robot training before retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot of these predictions never come true. At the depot we'd say they promised flying cars too. After church I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't believe a robot will do storm work on the headland in my lifetime, never mind by 2039. I'd be thirty-nine then. If it did happen, I'd have had a decade of good wages and hopefully a house paid down a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. Proper wedding, then we'd buy a small house in Kilbride in a couple of years, and start a family. I'd keep saving and keep my storm call-outs, because that overtime is what pays for the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a small knot in my stomach because it's still the same ending. But ten years is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't believe it'll happen. If you're wrong, what would you wish you'd done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saved more, probably. And maybe learned to drive the big machines, the cranes and the diggers, because someone has to deliver the robots. But I'm not doing that on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade, same as me, and to be good at it. But I'd also want them to be able to do something else, which I never had to think about. My dad didn't have to either.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and they promised flying cars too.
After church I'd say we'll **cross that bridge** when we come to it.
think: No robot will do **headland storm work** in my lifetime.
Even if it does, I'd have had **a decade of wages** and a part-paid house.
do: Have the **proper wedding**, then buy a small house in Kilbride.
Start a **family** within a few years.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small **knot** because the ending is the same.
S4.quote: I don't believe a robot will do storm work on the headland in my lifetime, never mind by 2039.
fieldNote: Wendy treats a ten-year warning as **too far off** to act on.
She admits she'd regret **not saving more**, but won't act on a guess.
For her children she wants a **trade plus a fallback**, something her family never needed.

steps.text: Keep taking storm overtime at the Kilbride depot
Buy a small house in Kilbride and start a family
Wait for real signs of robots before changing career plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and Rob's at the same time, and I'd have no idea what comes next. What would help is the company training its own people for the robots, picking from the crews, and keeping a few of us on for storms whatever happens. I'd want my family and the town to hold together, not a cheque from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the lights go out in our little coastal town, people know the crew by name, and if robots take that over, nobody counts what the town loses. You lose a bit of what makes a small town work.

headlineQuote: When the lights go out in our little coastal town, people know the crew by name, and if robots take that over, nobody counts what the town loses.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old third-generation lineworker** on a coastal depot crew, engaged to Rob, a mechanic.
She has **never used AI** and resents the forty-box tablet more than she fears storms.
In fast AGI she is **alarmed**, because robots would threaten both her and Rob's wages.
With more time she **waits to be picked** for training rather than chasing courses herself.
She values **family, parish and town** over government help and fears losing the crew's local role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would take her job and Rob's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: The company **training its own crews** for robots and keeping some on for storms.
**Family and town** holding together rather than a government cheque.
